\chapter{El Pedido Y La Devolución}
\label{ch:es-pedido}
\hlchaptermodality{431}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about an order that has arrived late, say who the shop blames, ask to return it and understand what I am being charged.}

Read the notice or advert this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el pedido]{el pedido — what you asked for}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-pedido}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{comprar} and \emph{la tienda}. Now say the \textbf{thing itself} — the parcel that has not arrived yet — and see whether you have a word for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el pedido}
\textbf{el pedido} — the order.

Not the act of ordering: the \textbf{thing ordered}. The box on its way to you, the line on the restaurant's docket, the number you quote on the phone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pedido} is the past participle of \textbf{pedir}, to ask for, used as a noun. What was asked for. Spanish does this constantly, and once you see it you will see it everywhere:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the noun made from it} \\
\midrule
pedir & el pedido \\
llamar & la llamada \\
entrar & la entrada \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You already hold \textbf{la entrada} for a ticket. It is \emph{the entered thing} by the same move. A participle that hardens into a noun is one of the cheapest ways this language makes new words, and it costs you no new ending.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pedido}
  \item I bought it in the shop, and the order has not arrived
  \item which verb \emph{el pedido} was made from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The order? (\textbf{el pedido}.) From which verb? (\textbf{pedir}.) Does it mean the asking or the thing asked for? (\textbf{The thing.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[devolver]{devolver — to turn it back}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-devolver}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pedido}. Say \emph{pagar}. The order came, you paid, and it is the wrong size. Say what you do next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: devolver}
\textbf{devolver} — to give back, to return a thing.

A thing, not a place. You \emph{devolver} a jumper, a book, a borrowed charger. For going back somewhere yourself, Spanish uses \textbf{volver} on its own.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{de-} back, plus \textbf{volver}, to turn. To turn a thing back.

That is the whole word, and it tells you the grammar too: \textbf{devolver} turns exactly like \textbf{volver}, which you already say. The \textbf{o} becomes \textbf{ue} when the stress lands on it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
yo devuelvo & I give back \\
nosotros devolvemos & we give back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The stress moves off the \textbf{o} in \emph{devolvemos}, and the \textbf{ue} goes with it. This is the same pattern as \emph{poder / puedo} and \emph{dormir / duermo}; learning it once buys you a whole family of verbs.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two ways back}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you mean} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
I return the order & devuelvo el pedido \\
I return home & vuelvo a casa \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English uses \emph{return} for both and lets context sort it out. Spanish splits them, and the split is not a nuisance — it is the prefix doing exactly what it says.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{devolver}
  \item I want to return the order
  \item I paid and now I am returning it
  \item the difference between \emph{devuelvo} and \emph{vuelvo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To give a thing back? (\textbf{devolver}.) And to go back yourself? (\textbf{volver}.) What does the \textbf{de-} add? (\textbf{Back.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el retraso]{el retraso — put further behind}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-retraso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pedido}. Say \emph{devolver}. The order is not late enough to return yet — it is only late. Say that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el retraso}
\textbf{el retraso} — the delay.

\textbf{con retraso} — late, running behind. That is the phrase you will hear on a platform: \emph{el tren sale con veinte minutos de retraso}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{re-} again, plus \textbf{tras}, behind. Something put further behind than it should be.

\textbf{tras} is worth a moment on its own, because it is hiding in words you will meet all week:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the behind in it} \\
\midrule
detrás & behind, in place \\
atrasar & to put back \\
el retraso & the being-behind \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish also has \textbf{tardar}, to take time, from a different Latin word for \emph{slow}. Two families, one idea, and a speaker picks whichever fits: a train \emph{lleva retraso}, a journey \emph{tarda} two hours.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el retraso}
  \item the order is arriving late
  \item the train leaves with twenty minutes' delay
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The delay? (\textbf{el retraso}.) Running late? (\textbf{con retraso}.) What does \textbf{tras} mean on its own? (\textbf{Behind.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el proveedor]{el proveedor — the one further up the line}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-proveedor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la tienda}. Say \emph{el retraso}. The shop says the delay is not their fault. Whose, then?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el proveedor}
\textbf{el proveedor} — the supplier.

The company that supplies the shop. You rarely deal with one; you hear about one when something has gone wrong: \emph{un problema con nuestro proveedor}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{proveer}, to provide, plus \textbf{-dor}, the ending that makes a doer.

That ending is worth more to you than this one word, because it is completely regular and it turns verbs you already hold into people and machines:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the doer} \\
\midrule
proveer & el proveedor \\
trabajar & el trabajador \\
vender & el vendedor \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Once you notice \textbf{-dor}, a long unfamiliar noun often decomposes into a verb you know plus \emph{the one who does it}. That is a reading strategy, not a word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el proveedor}
  \item there is a problem with the supplier
  \item the doer-word made from \emph{trabajar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The supplier? (\textbf{el proveedor}.) What does \textbf{-dor} add? (\textbf{The one who does it.}) From which verb? (\textbf{proveer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cobrar]{cobrar — the other end of paying}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-cobrar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{pagar}. Say \emph{el dinero}. You have had both a long time. Now say what the \textbf{shop} does, from its own side of the counter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cobrar}
\textbf{cobrar} — to charge somebody, to collect money, to get paid.

One verb for all three, and which one it means depends on who is speaking.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: who is on each end}]
\textbf{pagar} and \textbf{cobrar} are the same transaction from opposite sides:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{verb} \\
\midrule
the customer & paga \\
the shop & cobra \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{me cobraron treinta euros} — they charged me thirty. And \emph{cobro el viernes} — I get paid on Friday, said by somebody with a job. English needs three different verbs (\emph{charge}, \emph{collect}, \emph{get paid}) where Spanish holds one, and the one holds because the money is always moving \textbf{toward} the speaker.

That is also why \textbf{no se cobra nada} on a shop notice means nothing will be charged to you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cobrar}
  \item I pay and the shop charges
  \item they charged me thirty euros
  \item I get paid on Friday
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The customer does what? (\textbf{paga}.) And the shop? (\textbf{cobra}.) What does \emph{no se cobra nada} tell you? (\textbf{You will not be charged.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(pedido, devolver, retraso, proveedor …]{(pedido, devolver, retraso, proveedor, cobrar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R431-repaso-pedido}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{the order}, \emph{to give back} and \emph{the delay}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three of the five were built, not learned}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{made from} & \textbf{by} \\
\midrule
\textbf{el pedido} & pedir & a participle used as a noun \\
\textbf{el proveedor} & proveer & the doer-ending \textbf{-dor} \\
\textbf{devolver} & volver & the prefix \textbf{de-}, back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of this chapter's five words are a piece you already had plus one move. Do not read a rule into it — plenty of Spanish words are simple and whole. What is worth carrying is the habit of \textbf{looking} for the join before deciding a long word is new.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could buy things and pay for them, and you could not say what happens when it goes wrong.} \emph{Comprar}, \emph{pagar}, \emph{la tienda} and \emph{el dinero} have been yours for a long time, and between them they cover only the half of a transaction where everybody is content.

This chapter adds the other half: the thing itself (\textbf{el pedido}), it arriving late (\textbf{el retraso}), whose fault the shop says that is (\textbf{el proveedor}), sending it back (\textbf{devolver}) and what you are or are not charged (\textbf{cobrar}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item which three were built from a piece you already had
  \item the customer pays and the shop ...
  \item the order is arriving late and I want to return it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To give a thing back? (\textbf{devolver}.) The one who supplies the shop? (\textbf{el proveedor}.) The shop's side of \emph{pagar}? (\textbf{cobrar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(una reclamación) — the whole transaction, gone wrong}

\label{lesson:ES-C431-sintesis-reclamacion}



\begin{quote}
You are about to read a real notice of the kind a shop sends. Before you do, say \emph{el pedido} and \emph{el retraso} once each.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once without stopping, then answer.

\begin{quote}
Estimado cliente: su \textbf{pedido} número 3182 sufrirá un \textbf{retraso} de tres días por un problema con nuestro \textbf{proveedor}. No se le \textbf{cobrará} el envío.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item how many days late it is
  \item whose problem the shop says it is
  \item whether you will be charged for delivery
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now the other direction. Say aloud, as if on the telephone:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item my order is arriving with a delay of three days
  \item I paid on Monday and nobody has charged me for the delivery
  \item if it does not arrive this week I want to return it
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Four sentences ago you could not have said any of that.} The transaction you could describe stopped at the moment of paying; it now runs all the way to the complaint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Your order? (\textbf{mi pedido}.) With a delay? (\textbf{con retraso}.) And if you want to send it back? (\textbf{devolver}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
